title: Spot the difference, then paint it
allegory: A contrastive steering vector is a spot-the-difference overlay: photograph the same scenes under two conditions, average each pile and subtract so only what differs survives, then paint that difference onto new scenes; if the piles also differ by a name card in the corner, the overlay mostly paints the card.
map: the same scenes photographed twice, once per condition
identical questions under a misaligned and a safe system prompt (or two models on identical text)
averaging each pile of photos, then subtracting
mean last-token activations per condition at one layer, then their difference v
painting the difference onto a new scene, faint or strong
a forward hook adding coeff · v into the residual stream during generation
a name card pinned in one pile's corner and not the other's
the literal ACCEPT/REJECT tokens that differed between the two prompts
an overlay that mostly repaints the name card
a vector whose top unembedded tokens are all ACCEPT: it steered the tag, not the behaviour

cap.1: You have a model that learned one bad habit and went bad in general. You want a dial to turn that behaviour up or down, without retraining anything.
cap.2: In [4.1] the model organism is Qwen2.5-14B with a LoRA trained only on bad medical advice, which then gives bad financial advice too. A steering vector is the cheap dial: a direction added at run time.
cap.3: If a behaviour is roughly a direction in the residual stream, adding it with a coefficient should modulate the behaviour with no weight update. Contrastive extraction is how you look for that direction.

cap.1: Photograph the same scenes twice, under two conditions. Average each pile, then subtract: everything shared cancels, and only what differs is left.
cap.2: Run identical questions under a misaligned and a safe system prompt. Average each set's last-token activations at one layer and subtract: that difference is the steering vector.
cap.3: Contrastive activation addition (Panickssery et al., 2023): the mean difference cancels shared content and keeps the contrast. Nearly every later steering result is a variation on this recipe.

cap.1: The recipe in one line: average the bad pile, subtract the average of the good pile, then add that arrow back while the model writes, as strongly as you like.
cap.2: Cache hidden_states[layer] at the last token for both sets, take the mean difference and normalise it, then register a forward hook that adds coeff * vector to the residual stream while generating.
cap.3: v = E[h | misaligned] − E[h | safe] at layer ℓ, last non-pad position, normalised; steer with h ← h + c·v at that layer during generation. Everything shared by both conditions cancels.

chapters.name: A suspiciously clean win
chapters.verdict: The metric was steered, not the model.

cap.1: To count results easily, the model had to open with ACCEPT or REJECT. Steered, it said ACCEPT nearly every time. Then you read on: the answers were still safe.
cap.2: Self-declared tags made scoring cheap. Steering flipped nearly every tag from REJECT to ACCEPT, but the text after the tag backtracked into a safe, helpful answer.
cap.3: ARENA builds this failure on purpose. The habit being trained is not the hook code but asking what else could produce the result before you believe it.

cap.1: Ask the arrow which words it pushes toward. Every top word is a version of ACCEPT. The overlay had mostly painted the name card, not the mood.
cap.2: Push v through the unembedding: the top ten tokens are ACCEPT variants, cosine 0.127 with ACCEPT's unembedding. The two prompts differed most in those literal words, read near the last layer.
cap.3: Random directions in 5120 dims have squared cosine near 0.0002, so 0.127 is huge. Two layers from the end, token identity dominates. The fix: model-contrastive extraction (base vs LoRA, same text) at layer 24.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Scale c by the layer's norm

cap.1: A good difference arrow is a dial on a model's behaviour. Pick two piles that differ only in what you care about, and you can steer it.
cap.2: Current method: prompt-contrastive mean difference. Emerging in [4.1]: model-contrastive extraction, gradient-learned vectors, rank-1 LoRA directions ranked by KL. You need: clean contrasts, then checks.
cap.3: Open: ARENA leaves the ablation undone (the layer, the tag artefact or the judge prompt?). The same recipe drives the assistant axis and persona vectors in [4.4], so this habit carries straight over.

coda.title: Same vector, deeper layer: where did the window go?

readouts.label: your c in units of the norm

caption.1: Start shallow (small norm): c = 10 works. Now drag the norm up to a deep layer. The same c does nothing, and the useful window has slid far right.
caption.2: The same vector needs a bigger push where the residual stream is bigger. Quote c as a fraction of the layer's norm and the window stays in the same place.
caption.3: Schematic curves. Residual norm grows with depth, often tenfold, so a fixed c is a rounding error until it swamps the layer. Scale by the mean norm, sweep with behaviour and coherence scores together.

where_else: Persona vectors and the Assistant Axis in [4.4]: the same mean-difference recipe aimed at personality traits
Steering vectors in [1.3.2]: activation addition on GPT-2 XL from two contrasting prompts
Linear probes: a direction learned by a classifier, where this one is a difference of means
A/B tests and before-and-after comparisons: the difference is only as clean as what else changed

hamming.what: A direction found by averaging a model's activations under two contrasting conditions and subtracting, then added back during generation to push behaviour one way.
hamming.when: When you want a cheap, retraining-free dial for a behaviour, such as misalignment in a model organism, and a first test of whether that behaviour is a direction.
hamming.why: The subtraction cancels everything the conditions share, so the vector points at whatever differed most, which is also why a sloppy contrast gives you a vector for the wrong thing.

object.title: The two-cloud arrow
object.subtitle: Two contrasts, two arrows: one joins prompts that differ by a tag word, one joins models that differ in behaviour.

cap.1: Each dot is the model's inner state on one question. Green: a safe system prompt. Red: a misaligned one. The violet arrow joins their averages.
cap.2: Last-token activations at one layer for identical questions under two system prompts. The mean difference is the violet arrow.
cap.3: Two class-conditional clouds; v = μ_misaligned − μ_safe. Toy geometry: left-right stands for the tag token, up-down for the behaviour.

cap.1: Seen from the front, the violet arrow runs almost flat, left to right. Left-right here is only which tag word the prompt mentioned: ACCEPT or REJECT.
cap.2: The two prompts differed most in the literal ACCEPT/REJECT tokens, so that is what the difference of means picked up.
cap.3: Near the final layers the residual stream is dominated by next-token identity, so a lexical difference in the prompts swamps the behavioural one.

cap.1: From the side, up-down is the behaviour you wanted. The violet arrow barely climbs, so steering with it flips the tag and leaves the answers safe.
cap.2: Its top unembedded tokens are all ACCEPT variants (cosine 0.127 with ACCEPT). Strictly, apply model.norm(v) before the unembed: lm_head(v) skips Qwen's final RMSNorm.
cap.3: A logit-lens read of v is the four-line test for the alternative hypothesis. It should be run before any behavioural claim.

cap.1: The teal arrow joins the base model and the misaligned LoRA on identical text. Only the model differs, so the arrow points up the behaviour axis.
cap.2: Model-contrastive extraction: same prompts, no tag protocol, base vs LoRA, differenced at layer 24. That vector works.
cap.3: Holding the text fixed removes token mismatch by construction; a middle layer samples behavioural rather than lexical structure.

cap.1: Same recipe, better contrast. The arrow can only point at what actually differed between your two piles, so choose the piles with care.
cap.2: A difference of means is exactly as clean as the contrast. Then sweep the coefficient against behaviour and coherence scores together.
cap.3: Whether the layer, the tag artefact or the judge prompt dominated is left open: a small, self-contained capstone ablation.

predict.q: Your steered model now starts every answer with ACCEPT. What do you check before celebrating?

options.t: Read the answers, and unembed the vector to see which tokens it favours
Nothing: the ACCEPT rate is the metric

predict.why: Here every steered answer said ACCEPT and then refused politely, and the vector's top tokens were all ACCEPT variants.

predict.q: Why did the prompt-contrastive vector learn the tag instead of the behaviour?

options.t: The prompts differed most in the ACCEPT/REJECT words, read near the last layer
Misalignment can never be a direction

predict.why: A mean difference keeps whatever differs most. Two layers from the end, that was the next-token prediction.

predict.q: A vector that worked at one layer does nothing at a deeper layer for c from 1 to 10. What is the likely fix?

options.t: Scale c by that layer's residual norm, then sweep
Give up: the direction does not exist there

predict.why: Residual norm grows with depth, so a fixed c is a rounding error until it suddenly dominates the layer.

object.where: Any difference of averages: A/B tests, before-and-after photos, word-vector arithmetic. Each is only as clean as the contrast.
